# Status semantics: evidence first

The source documentation says C = paid off, 0 = 1-29 DPD, 1-4 = 30-149 DPD, 5 = 150+ DPD or written
off, X = no loan for the month. This page shows how each raw status actually behaves in consecutive
months (pairs whose month index differs by exactly 1), and the mapping implemented in
`sql/01_schema.sql` (`status_lookup`) and `src/utils/constants.py`.

## Findings

- **C is an absorbing exit, not CURRENT.** Of 419,324 transitions out of C,
  419,323 stay in C and 1 returns to an open status. C is reached from statuses 0-5
  20,241 times. A 'CURRENT' state that never deteriorates would give a degenerate
  roll-rate row; C is mapped to **PAID-OFF**.
- **X is a transient DORMANT state.** 18,737 clients (40.7%)
  start with X, so MOB is counted from the first non-X month. There are 27,660 exits from
  statuses 0-5 to X (12,183 clients) and 19,930 later re-entries;
  54% of exiting clients return. X is mapped to **DORMANT** and transitions through it
  are kept, never dropped.
- **0 behaves as the performing bucket.** Of clients with any non-X month, 96.1%
  start in 0. The source label 1-29 DPD is kept, and headline delinquency is measured at 30+.
- **5 is treated as absorbing, with anomalies reported.** On consecutive non-X rows, 5 is followed by a
  non-5 status 107 times out of 1,564
  (6.8%): 68 to C, 23 to 0,
  4 to 1, 7 to 2, 5 to 3, 0 to 4. They are written to
  `transition_anomalies`, excluded from every matrix, and the stress module reports a raw-leak sensitivity.

## Canonical mapping (STATE_MAPPING = evidence_based)

| Raw | State | Class |
|---|---|---|
| C | PAID-OFF | absorbing exit |
| X | DORMANT | transient, outside open book |
| 0 | 1-29 | open, transient |
| 1 | 30-59 | open, transient |
| 2 | 60-89 | open, transient |
| 3 | 90-119 | open, transient |
| 4 | 120-149 | open, transient |
| 5 | CHARGE-OFF | absorbing |

`source_literal` (C = CURRENT, X outside the book) is available only as the sensitivity view on the
Roll Rates page, which shows why it is degenerate.
